title: Where UK climate policy is on track — and where ministers need to act
label: 9 September 2026 · Progress on climate mitigation
summary: The Climate Change Committee (the CCC), an independent body that advises Parliament and audits progress on UK climate law, told MPs that the UK has made real progress on renewables and electric vehicles but faces risks on heat, industry, the grid, aviation and reliance on large-scale removals. The CCC defended a delayed publication of advice on Heathrow because of limited staff and busy statutory timetables, warned Ministers to speed up electrification and grid upgrades, urged cheaper electricity and clearer delivery plans for carbon removals and hydrogen, and flagged land-use and datacentre growth as emerging risks.

chapters.title: Role, delayed advice and resourcing
chapters.takeaway: The CCC says it must sometimes delay non-statutory advice because it is small and has heavy statutory duties, but MPs worried that delayed publication reduced Parliament’s chance to see independent views before consultations closed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Emma, please remind us what the Climate Change Committee does.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We’re the CCC — an independent adviser and auditor to Parliament and the devolved Governments on the UK Climate Change Act, carbon budgets, and adaptation. Our job is to check Government progress and give independent advice.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You were asked by the Transport Secretary for advice on the airports policy statement last November but your chair replied only in June and publication was timed after the consultation closed — why?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We had to fit extra work into a year with big statutory deadlines (our required climate risk and progress reports). We’re a small body, so timing and staff limits meant we couldn’t publish earlier in the consultation window.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: But that means Parliament and the public couldn’t see your independent view before the consultation closed. Isn’t that undermining your role to help Parliament hold Government to account?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: I appreciate the concern. We tried to move the timetable, and we’ll give MPs briefings and appear before the Transport Committee. Legally some statutory advice can’t be shared until it’s final, and we’re restricted by capacity.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should Parliament ask for better resourcing so you can respond faster?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We said we have resource limits. If the Committee wishes, the Chair can write to departments about ensuring the CCC has the capacity to deliver timely independent advice.

chapters.title: Headline progress and the priority: electrify faster
chapters.takeaway: The UK has strong wins — renewables and EV take-up — but to meet targets the CCC says ministers should speed up electrification and make electricity cheaper so households and businesses save money by switching.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: What would you tell the new Prime Minister and new ministers to prioritise this year?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Some good news: EV sales are booming — about 25% of new cars — renewable power auctions added 8.4 GW, and peatland restoration rose 24% year-on-year. But we need faster electrification: heat pumps, EVs and cheaper electricity.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: Why cheaper electricity?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Households with an EV, a heat pump, solar and a smart tariff could save roughly £1,200 a year versus staying on gas and petrol. Cheaper electricity reduces people’s bills and makes the switch attractive.

turns.speaker: Sojan Joseph
turns.text: The Prime Minister cut VAT on electricity. How much does that help?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: It helps a bit — Ofgem estimated the VAT cut was worth about £45 against otherwise higher bills — but the key metric is the price gap between electricity and gas. Right now electricity is about 3.3 times more expensive than gas; that gap must fall for fast electrification.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: The Government’s plan relies more on tech and removals than behaviour change. What risks does that create?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Relying heavily on unproven scale-up of removals or late tech means more risk — you need clear sector pathways, monitoring milestones and contingency plans if tech doesn’t deliver.

turns.speaker: Adrian Ramsay
turns.text: Does delaying decarbonisation cost more?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Yes. Our analysis shows every £1 spent on net zero returns roughly £2–£4 in benefits. Slower rollout delays those savings and exposes people to volatile fossil-fuel prices.

chapters.title: Transport, EVs and consumers
chapters.takeaway: The EV transition is working but fragile: stick to the zero-emission vehicle mandate, make charging cheaper and fairer, and help people who can’t charge at home.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: If the ZEV mandate is weakened, would uptake fall and targets be missed?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes. EVs are central to the Government’s pathway to 2030. Weakening the mandate risks failing the 2030 international pledge and undermining the UK’s delivery record.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Is the recent excise duty on EVs putting people off?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: We haven’t seen evidence yet. The planned EV excise is still much lower per mile than fuel duty, so running-cost savings mostly remain, especially if people can charge at home.

turns.speaker: Martin Rhodes
turns.text: Is access to charging unequal around the country?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes. London and Scotland lead; Northern Ireland lags. On-street low-power chargers grew slowest — but those are vital for people without driveways who charge overnight on cheap tariffs.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: Manufacturers have been heavily discounting to meet targets and face competition — is the mandate hurting UK industry and jobs?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Manufacturers worldwide face disruption. Important point: the UK mandate applies to cars sold here, not just built here; UK factories mainly export. Other markets also require EVs, so long-term demand exists.

turns.speaker: Sammy Wilson
turns.text: If fuel-duty revenue falls, won’t the State face a hole—forcing recovery through higher EV taxes and making EVs less attractive?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Possibly, but EVs still save running costs. Governments can manage revenues differently; they could phase in road pricing or higher excises later once the market is mature.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Let’s be blunt: people buy what’s cheapest overall. The policy task is to help manufacturers make affordable EVs and to ensure consumers can access savings — for example by expanding at-home and cheap public charging.

chapters.title: Buildings, heat pumps and practical barriers
chapters.takeaway: Rapid heat-pump rollout needs cheaper electricity, up-front cost support, more trained installers, and consumer protections so households aren't left with botched installs.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Warm Homes replaces ECO4. How do we avoid poor installs and make heat pumps affordable for low-income households?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: We need a well-designed scheme that bundles heat pumps with insulation, solar or batteries where needed, clear certification for installers, consumer protections and quick, standardised quotes.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: Air-to-air heat pumps are cheaper to install than air-to-water. Will including air-to-air help poorer households?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes — the Government extended grants to include air-to-air, which can cut install costs significantly and also give cooling benefits. But certified installers under the microgeneration scheme still need to be ready.

turns.speaker: Sarah Gibson
turns.text: What about the timing — people replace boilers when they break. Can the market respond quickly?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: That’s a real risk. We need enough installers, simpler consumer journeys and homeowner advice so replacements happen smoothly and quickly when boilers fail.

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Public buildings can lead by example. Right now there’s no dedicated public estate decarbonisation programme — investing in schools, hospitals and care homes would build market confidence and visibility.

chapters.title: Grid, datacentres, industry, hydrogen and carbon removals
chapters.takeaway: The CCC flags pressure on grid connections, huge new datacentre demand, industry electrification hurdles, delayed hydrogen and slow carbon capture rollout — ministers must set clear delivery plans, monitoring and contingencies.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You warned we must speed up grid connections but also future-proof them. Could rushing to meet 2030 create more upgrades later?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: You must do both. Build connections quickly but design for future demand, add storage, and use flexibility so you don't repeatedly upgrade lines — planning should combine networks and generation.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Datacentres are demanding huge connections — Ofgem recently flagged up to around 80 GW of connection requests — double our winter peak. Are you worried they’ll crowd out other users or run on fossil backup?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We used National Grid’s top estimates and included extra headroom in our modelling, so the scale is considered. But datacentres raise planning, water, and supply questions. If some sites run on on-site fossil generation while grid renewables are elsewhere, that poses a risk to meeting carbon budgets.

turns.speaker: Chris Hinchliff
turns.text: Could that fossil back-up blow our carbon budgets?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: It could become material if many large sites rely on local fossil generation. We’re keeping this under review and will give fuller advice in future work.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Industry electricity prices are still high. Will discounts alone drive electrification?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Discounts help some firms, but you also need capital support for big equipment, long-term industrial strategies, grid access, and skills. Cheap electricity is necessary but not sufficient.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: What about hydrogen and carbon capture — are we moving fast enough?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: We’re concerned. No contracts were awarded from Hydrogen Allocation Round 2 yet; delays hurt investor confidence. CCUS has about 70 plants worldwide as examples, and the UK has some funding (~£9bn so far) — but Government needs clearer delivery plans and more funding to hit the heavy reliance they assume.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: On aviation, sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is tiny — CCC reported 2.5% market share vs a target of 3.6% this year and 10% by 2030. What should Government do?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Keep to the mandate, diversify SAF routes (move beyond first-generation HEFA), and accelerate revenue-support mechanisms so investors build plants sooner. If tech or feedstocks lag, demand management will be needed as a contingency.

turns.speaker: Julia Buckley
turns.text: Are international offsets a big risk?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: Yes — the CCC wants strict criteria for any international credits used toward UK targets. For aviation we favour engineered removals that are permanent; cheap or low-quality credits risk undermining the whole plan.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: On land use: tree-planting rates have fallen and agriculture emissions haven’t budged much since 2008. Does the land use framework help?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: The framework and farming roadmap are positive but don’t yet guarantee delivery: payments and incentives must be long-term. UK tree planting needs to grow from ~15,000 ha/year in 2024–25 to ~35,000 ha/year by 2030 — that’s a big ramp-up needing stable funding and clear schemes across the UK.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Davies
turns.text: Should Government set a formal pathway to reduce livestock numbers?

turns.speaker: Emma Pinchbeck
turns.text: Our balanced pathway included some livestock change because shifting land use (trees, peat restoration) is part of a low-cost route to net zero. Governments can choose different mixes, but if livestock falls you must plan what to do with the land and support farmers through long-term incentives.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Finally, public understanding: should Government explain engineered removals better?

turns.speaker: Dr Devane
turns.text: The public needs to know practical things (EVs, heat pumps). But if the Government plans to spend large sums on engineered removals it must explain costs, timescales and, importantly, engage local communities where sites will be located.
